---
title: "Reporting an Analysis: From EDI Output to a Paper"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
render_start = Sys.time()
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

An analysis is not finished when the p-value prints. Someone has to turn the
output into a results table, write a methods section that says exactly what was
done, and record enough to let a reader (or you, a year later) rerun it. This
article goes from an EDI (Experimental Design and Inference) analysis to those
three things, and ends with how to cite the software and the design.

It assumes you know the four steps of an EDI analysis (design, assign, record
responses, infer) from [Get started](EDI.html) or the
[continuous cookbook](cookbook-continuous.html). The analysis below follows the
cookbook, so it is shown with little comment.

## 1. A worked analysis

Sixty subjects with three baseline covariates. Treatment is assigned by
rerandomization (Morgan and Rubin, 2012): candidate assignments with 30 treated
and 30 control are drawn by complete randomization, and only the 5% with the
smallest Mahalanobis imbalance in the covariate means are kept. The design gets
its own `seed`, so the assignment can be redrawn exactly.

```{r analysis}
set.seed(20261117)
n = 60
X = data.frame(
  age  = round(rnorm(n, 45, 12)),
  bmi  = round(rnorm(n, 27, 4), 1),
  male = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
)

design_seed = 7
prop_acceptable = 0.05
des = DesignFixedRerandomization$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous",
                                     prop_acceptable = prop_acceptable,
                                     objective = "mahal_dist",
                                     seed = design_seed, verbose = FALSE)
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des$get_w()

y = 10 + 2.5 * w + 0.1 * X$age - 0.3 * X$bmi + rnorm(n, sd = 3)
des$add_all_subject_responses(y)
```

`InferenceSuite` finds every inference class that applies to this design and
response, and `run_all_inference()` fits them. Here it is restricted to the three
mean-difference estimators (the unadjusted difference in means, OLS adjusted for
the covariates, and Lin's interacted regression) and to three procedures: the
Wald interval and test, the randomization test and interval, and the percentile
bootstrap. `compute_conf_intervals = TRUE` asks for intervals as well as
p-values; the default computes p-values only. The suite streams each row as it
finishes; that live output is hidden here and the finished results are printed
instead.

```{r suite, results = "hide"}
set.seed(1)
suite = InferenceSuite$new(des)
res = suite$run_all_inference(
  screen = TRUE, plots = FALSE, num_cores = 1L,
  classes = c("InferenceAllSimpleAverageDiff", "InferenceContinOLS", "InferenceContinLin"),
  methods = list(wald = NULL, rand = NULL, bootstrap = "percentile"),
  compute_conf_intervals = TRUE
)
```

```{r suite-print}
res
```

The last lines are a Cauchy-combined p-value across all nine rows. It is evidence
that at least one of these procedures found an effect; it is not an estimate and
does not belong in a results table as one (the
[`InferenceSuite`](../reference/InferenceSuite.html) help page explains why).

## 2. A results table

### From the suite

`res$results_table` is a plain `data.frame`, one row per class and procedure, with
the estimate, interval (`ci_a`, `ci_b`), p-value and the procedure's validity
regime. Pick the columns you need:

```{r suite-table}
tab = res$results_table[, c("inference_class", "method", "type", "estimate",
                            "ci_a", "ci_b", "pval", "regime")]
tab
```

`type` is filled in only for the resampling procedures that come in several
flavors (here the percentile bootstrap) and is `NA` for the others. Several
p-values equal 0.00399, which is 2/501: the smallest value the suite's
default 501 randomization or bootstrap draws can give (more on this below).

### From one inference object

More often a paper reports one pre-specified analysis, with one or two others as
sensitivity checks. Then it is simpler to fit that class directly and call the
procedures you will report. Each `compute_*_confidence_interval()` returns a
length-2 numeric vector and each `compute_*_two_sided_pval()` a single number, so
a table is a few lines:

```{r one-class}
inf = InferenceContinOLS$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
inf$num_cores = 1L
inf_seed = 1
inf$set_seed(inf_seed)

alpha = 0.05
r = 1000   # randomization draws
B = 501    # bootstrap draws

est = inf$compute_estimate()
ci_wald = inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = alpha)
p_wald  = inf$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
ci_rand = inf$compute_rand_confidence_interval(alpha = alpha, r = r, show_progress = FALSE)
p_rand  = inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = r, show_progress = FALSE)
ci_boot = inf$compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval(alpha = alpha, B = B, type = "bca",
                                                    show_progress = FALSE)
p_boot  = inf$compute_bootstrap_two_sided_pval(B = B, type = "bca",
                                               show_progress = FALSE)

results = data.frame(
  procedure = c("Wald (t)", "Randomization", "Bootstrap"),
  interval  = c("model-based SE",
                sprintf("test inversion, r = %d", r),
                sprintf("BCa, B = %d", B)),
  estimate  = est,
  lower     = c(ci_wald[1], ci_rand[1], ci_boot[1]),
  upper     = c(ci_wald[2], ci_rand[2], ci_boot[2]),
  p_value   = c(p_wald, p_rand, p_boot)
)
results
```

Both bootstrap numbers are BCa, the default type. BCa needs `B` of about 501 or
more; with fewer draws its adjusted tails land on the edge of the bootstrap
sample and the interval and p-value are `NA` with a warning, and
`type = "percentile"` is the choice if you need a small `B`.

For the paper, format it with `knitr::kable()` (or any table package). The one
thing to get right is the p-value from a resampling test: with `r` draws the
smallest p-value EDI reports is `2 / r`, so a value at that floor should be
printed as an upper bound, not as an exact number.

```{r kable}
fmt_p = function(p, floor = 0) {
  out = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)
  ifelse(p <= floor, paste0("≤ ", signif(floor, 2)), out)
}
pretty = data.frame(
  Procedure  = results$procedure,
  Interval   = results$interval,
  Estimate   = sprintf("%.2f", results$estimate),
  `95% CI`   = sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", results$lower, results$upper),
  p          = c(fmt_p(p_wald), fmt_p(p_rand, floor = 2 / r), fmt_p(p_boot, floor = 2 / B)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(pretty, align = "llrcr",
             caption = "Covariate-adjusted (OLS) treatment effect, three ways.")
```

### Which interval is which, and which to report

* **Wald (asymptotic).** Estimate plus or minus a critical value times a
  model-based standard error. For this OLS class it uses the t distribution.
  Valid as `n` grows; its error at a given `n` depends on the class and design.
* **Randomization.** The p-value tests the *sharp* null: treatment had no effect on
  any subject. It redraws the assignment `r` times from the design itself (here,
  from the accepted rerandomization assignments), so it is exact in finite samples
  up to Monte Carlo error. The interval inverts that test under a constant additive
  effect: it is the set of shifts `delta` the test does not reject.
* **Bootstrap.** Resamples subjects with their observed assignment `B` times.
  Percentile and BCa intervals have the same two-sided coverage order; BCa corrects
  for bias and skew. The bootstrap does not replay the rerandomization step.

The asymptotic and bootstrap tests are tests of a *weak* null: the average
treatment effect (here, the adjusted mean difference) is zero. The randomization
test is of the sharp null. Say which one you report; the two answer different
questions, and the difference matters most when effects vary across subjects.

The `regime` column in the suite table records this split (`"finite_sample"` vs
`"asymptotic"`), and `inf$get_procedure_validity()` gives, for every procedure,
the expected order of the size error and where that rate comes from. Which
procedure to trust at your sample size is the subject of
[Which procedure can I trust at my sample size?](procedure-trust.html), and the
simulation evidence behind each class is in
[Validation evidence](validation-evidence.html). Choose the primary procedure
before you see the data, put it in the protocol, and report the others as
sensitivity analyses. When they disagree, the table should show it.

## 3. A methods paragraph

A methods section needs enough detail for a reader to rerun the analysis. For an
EDI analysis, state:

* **The design and its parameters.** For rerandomization: the base randomization
  (complete, fixed arm sizes), the imbalance measure, and the acceptance rule
  (`prop_acceptable` or `obj_val_cutoff`). For a KK21 matching-on-the-fly design:
  `lambda` (the quantile cutoff for a match, default 10%) and `t_0_pct` (the share
  of subjects enrolled before matching starts, default 35%). For a blocked or
  stratified design: the blocking variables.
* **The estimand.** For example, the average treatment effect on the outcome scale,
  adjusted for named covariates; for other outcomes, an odds ratio, rate ratio or
  hazard ratio.
* **The test and its null.** Sharp null (randomization tests) or weak null
  (asymptotic, likelihood and bootstrap tests); two-sided; `alpha`.
* **The interval type and the number of draws.** Wald, randomization (with `r`),
  bootstrap (BCa or percentile, with `B`).
* **The seeds.** The design seed and the inference seed.
* **The software.** R and EDI versions (`packageVersion("EDI")`) and the
  citation (`citation("EDI")`).

Writing the paragraph with inline R code keeps every number in it tied to the
objects that produced it. In the R Markdown source, the start of the paragraph
below reads

```markdown
A total of `r knitr::inline_expr("n")` participants were assigned to treatment
(n = `r knitr::inline_expr("n_T")`) or control (n = `r knitr::inline_expr("n_C")`) by rerandomization ...
```

where `n_T` and `n_C` are computed in a hidden chunk from `des$get_w()`. Every
number in it comes from the objects above:

```{r methods-values, include = FALSE}
n_T = sum(w)
n_C = n - n_T
covs = names(X)
rand_p_text = if (p_rand <= 2 / r) {
  sprintf("p ≤ %s", format(2 / r))
} else {
  sprintf("p = %s", format(signif(p_rand, 2)))
}
r_version = paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")
edi_cite_year = citation("EDI")$year
```

> **Methods.** A total of `r n` participants were assigned to treatment (n =
> `r n_T`) or control (n = `r n_C`) by rerandomization (Morgan and Rubin, 2012).
> Candidate assignments were drawn by complete randomization with equal arm sizes,
> and the `r 100 * prop_acceptable`% with the smallest Mahalanobis distance between
> the treated and control means of `r paste(covs, collapse = ", ")` were accepted;
> the assignment used was one draw from that accepted set (design seed
> `r design_seed`). The estimand was the average treatment effect on the outcome,
> estimated by ordinary least squares regression of the outcome on treatment and
> `r paste(covs, collapse = ", ")`. The primary analysis was a two-sided
> randomization test of the sharp null hypothesis of no treatment effect for any
> participant, using `r format(r, big.mark = ",")` assignments redrawn from the same
> rerandomization design, at level `r alpha`. The
> `r 100 * (1 - alpha)`% confidence interval was obtained by inverting this test
> under a constant additive treatment effect. As sensitivity analyses we report the
> Wald interval based on the model standard error and a BCa bootstrap interval
> (`r B` resamples of participants). Resampling used seed `r inf_seed`. Analyses were
> run in R `r r_version` with the EDI package, version
> `r as.character(packageVersion("EDI"))` (Kapelner, `r edi_cite_year`).
>
> **Results.** The estimated treatment effect was `r sprintf("%.2f", est)`
> (95% randomization CI `r sprintf("%.2f", ci_rand[1])` to
> `r sprintf("%.2f", ci_rand[2])`; randomization `r rand_p_text`). The Wald interval
> was `r sprintf("%.2f", ci_wald[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", ci_wald[2])` and the BCa
> bootstrap interval `r sprintf("%.2f", ci_boot[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", ci_boot[2])`.

Two things in it deserve a sentence in any methods section. First, the
randomization test used the design that was actually run: redrawing from complete
randomization instead would ignore the acceptance rule and give the wrong
reference distribution. Second, the primary procedure is named, and the others are
labeled sensitivity analyses, so a reader does not have to guess which p-value
was planned.

## 4. What to record for reproducibility

Rerunning an EDI analysis exactly needs the data, the code, the seeds and the
software versions. Two details are specific to EDI:

* **Both seeds.** The design `seed` fixes the assignment. The inference object's
  `set_seed()` fixes its randomization and bootstrap draws. Without it, the
  randomization draws fall back to the design seed and the bootstrap follows R's
  global RNG state, so a `set.seed()` call before the analysis is then part of
  the record. Record every seed you set.
* **The design object itself.** It holds the covariates, the assignment, the
  responses and the design settings. Saving it with `saveRDS()` lets anyone rerun
  every inference procedure on exactly the assignment that was used, without
  redrawing it:

```{r save-design}
design_file = tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(des, design_file)

des_reloaded = readRDS(design_file)
identical(des_reloaded$get_w(), des$get_w())

inf_reloaded = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_reloaded, verbose = FALSE)
inf_reloaded$num_cores = 1L
inf_reloaded$set_seed(inf_seed)
all.equal(inf_reloaded$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = r, show_progress = FALSE), p_rand)
```

In a real project, write the file next to the data rather than to a temporary
directory. Record the versions too: `packageVersion("EDI")` here is
`r as.character(packageVersion("EDI"))`, and the design object stores the version
that created it (`des$get_edi_version_created()`), as does the suite result
(`res$edi_version`). `sessionInfo()` covers R and every other package.

How seeds reach each procedure, and which procedures give the same result at
any number of cores, is covered in [Reproducibility](reproducibility.html).

## 5. How to cite EDI and the design

Cite the software:

```{r citation}
citation("EDI")
```

`toBibtex(citation("EDI"))` gives the BibTeX entry. The citation records the
installed version, which should match the version in your methods section.

Also cite the paper behind the design you used, and the paper behind the
estimator where there is one. The package's
[`REFERENCES.md`](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI/blob/main/R/EDI/REFERENCES.md)
file lists each reference with the classes that use it. For the designs most often used with EDI:

* **Rerandomization** (`DesignFixedRerandomization`): Morgan, K. L., and Rubin,
  D. B. (2012). Rerandomization to improve covariate balance in experiments.
  *The Annals of Statistics*, 40(2), 1263-1282.
  [doi:10.1214/12-AOS1008](https://doi.org/10.1214/12-AOS1008).
* **KK21 matching on the fly** (`DesignSeqOneByOneKK21`): Kapelner, A., and
  Krieger, A. M. (2023). A matching procedure for sequential experiments that
  iteratively learns which covariates improve power. *Biometrics*, 79(1), 216-229.
  [doi:10.1111/biom.13561](https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.13561).
* **KK14 matching on the fly** (`DesignSeqOneByOneKK14`, and the matched-pair
  plus reservoir estimators): Kapelner, A., and Krieger, A. M. (2014). Matching
  on-the-fly: Sequential allocation with higher power and efficiency.
  *Biometrics*, 70(2), 378-388.
  [doi:10.1111/biom.12148](https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.12148).

Each design's help page (for example `?DesignFixedRerandomization`) names its
source in the References section.
